newsitem.title: USA: Gene map spurs research, education.
newsitem.headline: Gene map spurs research, education.

text.p: A map of about 16,000 human genes can now be seen on the Internet, part of a project to teach students and the public about heredity while helping scientists speed up the search for disease-causing genes.

In collaboration with laboratories and scientists around the world, the U.S. National Library of Medicines at the National Institutes of Health introduced the gene map on an Internet web site on Thursday. It also appears on Friday in the journal Science.

Although genes have been mapped and data published in different forms, scientists said this was an unprecedented effort to provide a map of the location of 16,334 genes identified so far that would be accessible to laypeople and scientists alike.

Only a small portion of those genes are fully understood, but mapping them on the chromosomes is a key step. Genes, made up of segments of DNA, contain the instructions for how cells should behave. Genes are found along 23 pairs of chromosomes in the cell nucleus.
Dr. Francis Collins, director of the National Centre for Human Genome Research, called the map project placing "bookmarks in the book of life."

Like many web sites, this one has a multi-layered format with a simple menu of choices. One click of the mouse can provide very basic, easy-to-understand information about Alzheimer's disease or juvenile diabetes, for example, and lists resources for patients.
Another click can give scientists state-of-the-art information on the hunt for related genes and their functions that can vastly accelerate the process of finding specific genes linked to illnesses.
"It is particularly useful to the gene hunter," said Collins. "This can enormously speed up the process of finding disease genes."

"We have all these pieces of the puzzle lying around, we have no idea where they are (in the puzzle)," Eric Landler, director of the Whitehead Centre for Biomedical Research's genome project, told reporters earlier this week.
He said the new map consolidates lots of data and gene sequencing information from labs around the world and makes it more usable for gene hunters.

Scientists believe there are about 50 to 100,000 genes in the human genome, with the number 80,000 often cited as a sensible middle estimate. The goal of the six-year-old international Human Genome Project is to be able to find the location of all the genes, and read the roughly three billion pieces of information in their genetic script, by 2005.

In some cases, like Alzheimer's Disease or Huntington's, doctors cannot yet do much with the genetic information. But with others, like certain colon cancers, people with gene defects can be carefully monitored and take preventive steps.
And researchers believe that decoding the genome will soon lead to a new era of molecular medicine and new ways of treating thousands of diseases.

The debut of the map on the web coincides with a series of reports in Science that reviews the advances of the genome project, as well as some of the troubling ethical and social implications of genetic research.

A Georgetown University survey, also reported on Friday in Science, found that many people in families at risk for hereditary disorders believe they are facing discrimination from insurers or risk losing their jobs if they shared their genetic information with employers.
